reels.title: The Man Who Talks to Houses
reels.hook_text: 8 years in Petersburg. Not one friend.
reels.hook_vo: It was a wonderful night, such a night as is only possible when we are young, dear reader.

script.text: It was a wonderful night, such a night as is only possible when we are young, dear reader.
But all that day he had been sinking into a strange gloom.
It suddenly seemed to me that I was lonely, that every one was forsaking me and going away from me.
For though I had been living almost eight years in Petersburg I had hardly an acquaintance.
Instead, he befriends strangers he has never spoken to, like one old man on the Fontanka.
That is how it is that we almost bow to each other, especially when we are both in good humour.
And he is friends with the buildings.
I know the houses too. As I walk along they seem to run forward in the streets to look out at me from every window
His favourite was a pretty pink house. Then last week:
I heard a plaintive, “They are painting me yellow!” The villains! The barbarians!
So why, after eight years of this, does the whole city suddenly feel like it is abandoning him?

reels.title: The City Forgot Him
reels.hook_text: POV: the whole city left without you
reels.hook_vo: Aie! Why, they are giving me the slip and making off to their summer villas!

script.text: Aie! Why, they are giving me the slip and making off to their summer villas!
For three days something felt wrong. Then it hit him: it is summer, and all Petersburg is leaving town.
Wagons piled with sofas. Boats loaded with furniture. In his eyes, a hundred times over.
It seemed as though Petersburg threatened to become a wilderness, so that at last I felt ashamed, mortified and sad that I had nowhere to go for the holidays and no reason to go away.
I was ready to go away with every waggon, to drive off with every gentleman of respectable appearance who took a cab; but no one — absolutely no one — invited me;
So he walked, and walked, until he found himself outside the city gates.
It was as though I had suddenly found myself in Italy — so strong was the effect of nature upon a half-sick townsman like me, almost stifling between city walls.
He heads home happy, late that night. But on the canal, something is waiting for him.

reels.title: A Girl at the Railing
reels.hook_text: 10 p.m. A stranger crying alone on the canal.
reels.hook_vo: And yet my night was better than my day! This was how it happened.

script.text: And yet my night was better than my day! This was how it happened.
First, a strange thought: spring in Petersburg reminds him of
a frail, consumptive girl, at whom one sometimes looks with compassion
who flares into beauty for one instant, then fades.
And you grieve that the momentary beauty has faded so soon never to return, that it flashed upon you so treacherously, so vainly, grieve because you had not even time to love her. . . .
Remember that image. Now: ten o'clock, the empty canal embankment.
I walked along singing, for when I am happy I am always humming to myself like every happy man who has no friend or acquaintance with whom to share his joy.
Leaning on the canal railing stood a woman with her elbows on the rail,
She was wearing a very charming yellow hat and a jaunty little black mantle.
I heard a muffled sob. Yes! I was not mistaken, the girl was crying,
He is terrified of women. She is in tears. Will he dare to speak to her?

reels.title: The Knotted Stick
reels.hook_text: He almost said 'Madam!' Then fate stepped in.
reels.hook_vo: And timid as I was with women, yet this was such a moment!

script.text: And timid as I was with women, yet this was such a moment!
I turned, took a step towards her, and should certainly have pronounced the word “Madam!” if I had not known that that exclamation has been uttered a thousand times in every Russian society novel.
Too late. She slips past him and crosses the street.
I dared not cross the street after her. My heart was fluttering like a captured bird.
A drunk gentleman in evening dress staggers out of the dark, and gives chase.
The girl uttered a shriek, and . . . I bless my luck for the excellent knotted stick, which happened on that occasion to be in my right hand.
“Give me your arm,” I said to the girl. “And he won’t dare to annoy us further.”
On her black eyelashes there still glistened a tear — from her recent terror or her former grief — I don’t know.
Her former grief. So what was she crying about before any of this happened?

reels.title: Twenty-Six and Never Spoken to a Woman
reels.hook_text: He's 26. He has never talked to a woman.
reels.hook_vo: Yes; if my arm trembles, it is because it has never been held by a pretty little hand like yours.

script.text: Yes; if my arm trembles, it is because it has never been held by a pretty little hand like yours.
She noticed he was trembling. So he confesses everything.
Here, I am twenty-six and I have never seen any one.
I don’t know how to be silent when my heart is speaking.
Believe me, not one woman, never, never! No acquaintance of any sort! And I do nothing but dream every day that at last I shall meet some one.
Oh, if only you knew how often I have been in love in that way. . . .
In love? With whom?
Why, with no one, with an ideal, with the one I dream of in my sleep.
He has even imagined stopping a lady in the street to beg her for
two or three sisterly words with sympathy
should laugh at me if she likes, encourage me, say two words to me, only two words, even though we never meet again afterwards!
She is laughing now. But is she laughing at him, or with him?

reels.title: 'Surely This Is Not the End?'
reels.hook_text: Why did you really come up to me?
reels.hook_vo: Don’t be vexed; I am only laughing at your being your own enemy,

script.text: Don’t be vexed; I am only laughing at your being your own enemy,
No kind-hearted woman, unless she were stupid or, still more, vexed about something at the moment, could bring herself to send you away without those two words which you ask for so timidly.
Then she presses him: why did he really approach her?
I fancied you were crying, and I . . . could not bear to hear it . . . it made my heart ache.
They reach her street. She says goodbye.
Surely . . . surely you don’t mean . . . that we shall never see each other again? . . . Surely this is not to be the end?

I tell you what, I can’t help coming here to-morrow, I am a dreamer; I have so little real life that I look upon such moments as this now, as so rare, that I cannot help going over such moments again in my dreams.
I shall be dreaming of you all night, a whole week, a whole year.
He will be back tomorrow at ten. But will she?

reels.title: Rule One: Don't Fall in Love
reels.hook_text: Her one condition: don't fall in love with me.
reels.hook_vo: She agrees to meet him again. But there's a catch.

perhaps I will come here to-morrow, too, at ten o’clock.
The fact is, I have to be here; don’t imagine that I am making an appointment with you;
you won’t fall in love with me. . . . That’s impossible, I assure you. I am ready for friendship; here’s my hand. . . . But you mustn’t fall in love with me, I beg you!

Hush, don’t swear, I know you are ready to flare up like gunpowder.
And she has a secret, something she might confide in him.
Wait till to-morrow. Meanwhile, let that be a secret. So much the better for you; it will give it a faint flavour of romance.
In two minutes you have made me happy for ever.
And we parted. I walked about all night; I could not make up my mind to go home. I was so happy. . . . To-morrow!

reels.title: The Man With No History
reels.hook_text: Night 2. 'Tell me your whole history.'
reels.hook_vo: Well, so you have survived!

script.text: Well, so you have survived!
I’ve been here for the last two hours; you don’t know what a state I have been in all day.
But she has decided to be sensible. She realises she knows nothing about him.
Well, what sort of man are you? Come, make haste — begin — tell me your whole history.
My history! But who has told you I have a history? I have no history.
Then how have you lived, if you have no history?
Absolutely without any history! I have lived, as they say, keeping myself to myself, that is, utterly alone — alone, entirely alone.
She tries to guess. Maybe he has a grandmother like hers:
She is blind and will never let me go anywhere,
she called me up and pinned my dress to hers, and ever since we sit like that for days together;
Very well, I am a type!
A type? What on earth is a type? He is about to explain, and it will take a while.

My name is Nastenka.

There are, Nastenka, though you may not know it, strange nooks in Petersburg.
In these corners, dear Nastenka, quite a different life is lived,

reels.title: Half Man, Half Tortoise
reels.hook_text: Dostoevsky: a dreamer is not a human being.
reels.hook_vo: The dreamer — if you want an exact definition — is not a human being, but a creature of an intermediate sort.

once he slips into his corner, he grows to it like a snail, or, anyway, he is in that respect very much like that remarkable creature, which is an animal and a house both at once, and is called a tortoise.
And when a rare friend visits? Panic. Awkward silence. The friend grabs his hat and flees, never to return. The host looks
as though he had only just committed some crime within his four walls;
like

Nastenka stares at him, mouth open.
all I know is, that this adventure must have happened word for word to you.
“Doubtless,” I answered, with the gravest face.
You talk as though you were reading it out of a book.
at this moment a thousand valves have opened in my head, and I must let myself flow in a river of words, or I shall choke.

script.text: There is, my friend Nastenka, one hour in my day which I like extremely.

for one feels awfully ashamed to tell it in the first person
walks the canal with a strange smile.
He is rich now with his own individual life;
Now ‘the Goddess of Fancy’ (if you have read Zhukovsky, dear Nastenka) has already with fantastic hand spun her golden warp and begun weaving upon it patterns of marvellous magic life
He forgets where he is. Strangers laugh at him. He doesn't even notice eating dinner. Then darkness falls in his room.
his soul is sad and empty; the whole kingdom of fancies drops to pieces about him,
Until a new dream stirs.

of a little home of one’s own and beside one a dear creature who listens to one on a winter’s evening, opening her little mouth and eyes as you are listening to me now, my angel. . . .
Would you believe, looking at him, dear Nastenka, that he has never known her whom he loves in his ecstatic dreams?
In the dream she was trapped with a gloomy old husband. Years later he finds her at a masked ball in the south, where
she hurriedly removes her mask and whispering, ‘I am free,’ flings herself trembling into his arms,
And right at that moment, a cheerful friend bursts through the door.
‘My dear boy, I have this minute come from Pavlovsk.’ My goodness! the old count is dead, unutterable happiness is close at hand — and people arrive from Pavlovsk!

reels.hook_text: She didn't laugh. She asked one question.
reels.hook_vo: Surely you haven’t lived like that all your life?

He expected her to burst out laughing. Instead, she pressed his hand.
“All my life, Nastenka,” I answered; “all my life, and it seems to me I shall go on so to the end.”
“No, that won’t do,” she said uneasily, “that must not be;
“I know, Nastenka, I know!” I cried, unable to restrain my feelings longer.
“And I realize now, more than ever, that I have lost all my best years!
what shall I have to dream of when I have been so happy in reality beside you!
Oh, may you be blessed, dear girl, for not having repulsed me at first, for enabling me to say that for two evenings, at least, I have lived.
“Oh, no, no!” cried Nastenka and tears glistened in her eyes.
what are two evenings?

Oh, Nastenka, Nastenka! If only you knew how lonely I am now!
Next day: rain. She doesn't come. He walks to her street, then turns back at her door.
But to-morrow, to-morrow! To-morrow she will tell me everything.
They are together by now. . . .
Is he right? Night 4 will answer everything.

script.text: My God, how it has all ended! What it has all ended in!
she was standing as she had been that first time, with her elbows on the railing,
Well, where is the letter? Have you brought the letter?
“No, there is no letter,” I said at last. “Hasn’t he been to you yet?”
She turned fearfully pale and looked at me for a long time without moving. I had shattered her last hope.
“Well, God be with him,” she said at last in a breaking voice; “God be with him if he leaves me like that.”
And not a line, not a line! He might at least have written that he does not want me, that he rejects me — but not a line for three days!
When I think that I was the first to go to him, that I humbled myself before him, cried, that I begged of him a little love!
She is falling apart. And the Dreamer is about to make it worse, or better.

reels.title: 'I Love You, Nastenka'
reels.hook_text: Four nights. One rule. He's about to break it.
reels.hook_vo: Four nights ago, she made him promise not to fall in love. Tonight, he breaks it.

script.text: Four nights ago, she made him promise not to fall in love. Tonight, he breaks it.
He offers to go to the man himself. She refuses.
I don’t know him; I don’t love him any more. I will . . . forget him.
Tell me: you wouldn’t have behaved like this, would you? You would not have abandoned a girl who had come to you of herself,
Nastenka, you torture me! You wound my heart, you are killing me, Nastenka! I cannot be silent!
What I am going to say to you now is all nonsense, all impossible, all stupid! I know that this can never be, but I cannot be silent.
“What is it? What is it?” she said drying her tears and looking at me intently,
It’s impossible, but I love you, Nastenka! There it is! Now everything is told,
He has said it. Now, how will she react?

script.text: What of it? I knew you loved me long ago, only I always thought that you simply liked me very much.

Here my tears are falling, Nastenka. Let them flow, let them flow — they don’t hurt anybody. They will dry, Nastenka.
He means to leave and never see her again. But first:
I thought that you . . . I thought that you somehow . . . quite apart from me, had ceased to love him.
only I would love you, I would love you so, that even if you still loved him, even if you went on loving the man I don’t know, you would never feel that my love was a burden to you.
You would only feel every minute that at your side was beating a grateful, grateful heart,
Oh Nastenka, Nastenka! What have you done to me?

reels.title: Will You Take My Hand?
reels.hook_text: She asked him one thing: can you wait?
reels.hook_vo: Stay, listen to me: can you wait?

script.text: Stay, listen to me: can you wait?
He had tried to leave. She stopped him.
I love him; but I shall get over it, I must get over it, I cannot fail to get over it;
for you love me while he has never loved me, for in fact, I love you myself. . . . Yes, I love you!
she laid her head upon my shoulder, then upon my bosom, and wept bitterly.
I have loved him for a whole year, and I swear by God that I have never, never, even in thought, been unfaithful to him.
for I can only love what is magnanimous, what understands me, what is generous;
if you are ready to love me always as you do now — I swear to you that gratitude . . . that my love will be at last worthy of your love. . . . Will you take my hand?
“Nastenka!” I cried breathless with sobs. “Nastenka, oh Nastenka!”
The Dreamer finally has a real life. How long can it last?

I am poor, I have only got twelve hundred roubles, but that doesn’t matter.
Of course not, and granny has her pension, so she will be no burden. We must take granny.
Of course we must take granny. But there’s Matrona.
He will rent the empty room upstairs, just like the last lodger.
So by to-morrow you will be my lodger.
And we will go to The Barber of Seville, for they are soon going to give it again.
“Yes, we’ll go,” said Nastenka, “but better see something else and not The Barber of Seville.”
They wander in a happy daze. At last he walks her home.
Look at the sky, Nastenka. Look! To-morrow it will be a lovely day; what a blue sky, what a moon!
But Nastenka did not look at the cloud; she stood mute as though turned to stone;
Something has frozen her. What did she just see?

reels.hook_text: The man she waited a year for. Right now.
reels.hook_vo: At that moment a young man passed by us.

script.text: At that moment a young man passed by us.
He suddenly stopped, looked at us intently, and then again took a few steps on. My heart began throbbing.
“Who is it, Nastenka?” I said in an undertone.
“It’s he,” she answered in a whisper,
huddling up to me, still more closely, still more tremulously. . . . I could hardly stand on my feet.
Nastenka, Nastenka! It’s you!
My God, how she cried out! How she started! How she tore herself out of my arms and rushed to meet him! I stood and looked at them, utterly crushed.
she turned to me again, was beside me again in a flash, and before I knew where I was she threw both arms round my neck and gave me a warm, tender kiss.
Then, without saying a word to me, she rushed back to him again, took his hand, and drew him after her.
I stood a long time looking after them. At last the two vanished from my sight.
Not a word. Just a kiss. Will she ever explain?

reels.hook_text: The morning after. A letter from her.
reels.hook_vo: My night ended with the morning.

script.text: My night ended with the morning.
It was a wet day. The rain was falling and beating disconsolately upon my window pane;
“There’s a letter for you, sir; the postman brought it,” Matrona said stooping over me.
I broke the seal. It was from her!
Oh, forgive me, forgive me! I beg you on my knees to forgive me! I deceived you and myself. It was a dream, a mirage. . . .
Oh, my God! If only I could love you both at once! Oh, if only you were he!
“Oh, if only he were you,” echoed in my mind.
For it will live in my memory like a sweet dream which lingers long after awakening;
Next week I am to be married to him. He has come back in love, he has never forgotten me.
Forgive me, remember and love your “NASTENKA.”
I read that letter over and over again for a long time; tears gushed to my eyes.
Married next week. So what is left for the Dreamer, and can he forgive her?

reels.title: A Whole Moment of Happiness
reels.hook_text: The last line of this book will wreck you.
reels.hook_vo: I have taken all the cobwebs off the ceiling; you can have a wedding or give a party.

script.text: I have taken all the cobwebs off the ceiling; you can have a wedding or give a party.
Matrona means well. But as he looks at her, everything ages.
I don’t know why I suddenly pictured my room grown old like Matrona.
I saw myself just as I was now, fifteen years hence, older, in the same room, just as solitary, with the same Matrona grown no cleverer for those fifteen years.
And yet, no bitterness.
But to imagine that I should bear you a grudge, Nastenka!

Oh never, never! May your sky be clear, may your sweet smile be bright and untroubled, and may you be blessed for that moment of blissful happiness which you gave to another, lonely and grateful heart!
My God, a whole moment of happiness! Is that too little for the whole of a man’s life?
